title: Water
introduction: How can the same small molecule keep a plant connected, dissolve a nutrient and shape an animal’s habitat?

sections.explanation:
Think of a seed after rain: water makes movement and chemical change possible inside living cells. The earliest cells arose in an aqueous environment. Water remains the medium for most cellular processes, including many enzyme-catalysed reactions.

The cytosol is the aqueous part of the cytoplasm. Dissolved substances can move through it and meet reaction partners. Water also carries solutes between parts of an organism: mineral ions travel in xylem sap, and many substances travel in blood plasma. A medium is the surrounding environment in which a process occurs; it need not be the reactant in every reaction.

Life depends on both an aqueous phase and organized boundaries. Hydrophobic regions of membrane lipids help separate cells from their surroundings. Water enables many processes but does not, by itself, create a living cell.

In a dry mixture, many reactants cannot move freely enough to meet. In an aqueous phase, dissolved particles move randomly and diffusion can bring a substrate to an enzyme. Dissolving is not the same as reacting: water provides the setting, while the enzyme lowers the activation barrier. Some enzymes are attached to membranes rather than freely dissolved; they still operate in a hydrated environment.
sections.revisionSummary: Early cells arose in water. Most cellular chemistry still occurs in an aqueous medium; water also supports transport.
terms: Medium: environment in which a process occurs
sections.workedExample: An enzyme and its soluble substrate can meet in cytosol. The surrounding water allows movement; the enzyme provides catalysis.

sections.activityTitle: What does water actually make possible?

sections.explanation:
Each water molecule contains an oxygen atom covalently bonded to two hydrogen atoms. Oxygen attracts shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does. Electron sharing is unequal: oxygen has a partial negative charge (δ−), while each hydrogen has a partial positive charge (δ+). These are partial charges, not full ionic charges.

Water has a bent shape, so the two polar O–H bonds do not cancel one another’s charge separation. The molecule is polar overall, although its total electrical charge is zero. In the figure, solid lines represent the polar covalent bonds within each molecule.

A hydrogen bond can form between the δ+ hydrogen bonded to oxygen in one molecule and the oxygen of a neighboring molecule. Dashes mark this intermolecular attraction. Do not connect two oxygens with a covalent bond, or describe the hydrogen bond as shared electrons between the two water molecules. In liquid water this network continually rearranges.

Follow three separate steps: oxygen attracts the shared electron pairs more strongly; this creates partial charges within a bent molecule; opposite partial charges on neighbouring molecules permit hydrogen bonding. Electrons are not completely transferred from hydrogen to oxygen. Heating liquid water can disrupt and rearrange hydrogen bonds without splitting each H₂O molecule into hydrogen and oxygen.
sections.revisionSummary: Unequal sharing + bent shape → molecular polarity → hydrogen bonding between molecules. Solid O–H lines are covalent; dashed H···O lines are hydrogen bonds.
terms: Hydrogen bond: attraction involving a bonded hydrogen and a suitable acceptor

sections.exampleTitle: Read the two kinds of bond

sections.explanation:
Cohesion is attraction between molecules of the same substance. In water, hydrogen bonds provide an important contribution. A pull on one part of a continuous water column can be transmitted to neighboring molecules.

In xylem, evaporation from leaves produces tension: water is under a pulling force. Cohesion helps the water column remain continuous as that tension is transmitted down the plant. This supports upward mass flow from roots. It is a cohesion–tension mechanism, not an active pump in each xylem vessel; broken columns can interrupt transport.

At a water–air boundary, cohesive interactions give rise to surface tension: increasing the surface area costs energy. Small water striders can use the surface as a habitat because their water-repellent legs distribute their weight without rupturing it. The surface is deformable; it is not a solid skin.

Trace the pull from the leaf towards the root. Evaporation removes water from moist cell-wall surfaces in the leaf. Replacement water is drawn from the xylem, lowering its pressure and putting the continuous liquid column under tension. Cohesive attractions transmit that tension. The energy driving this process comes from evaporation, rather than from hydrogen bonds acting as an energy source.
sections.revisionSummary: Hydrogen bonding → cohesion → transmission of tension in xylem and surface tension at the water–air interface.
terms: Surface tension: tendency of a liquid surface to resist increasing area
sections.workedExample: A water strider spreads its load across long legs. Cohesion contributes to a surface that can support that small load.

sections.activityTitle: Predict what happens to the water column

sections.explanation:
Adhesion is attraction between different substances. Polar water molecules interact with polar or charged groups on a suitable surface, including components of plant cell walls. Cohesion is water–water attraction; adhesion is water–surface attraction.

In a narrow wettable pore, adhesion and surface tension can draw water upward or along the pore. Cohesion helps the liquid move together. The curved meniscus indicates wetting. Under otherwise similar conditions, a narrower pore can support a greater capillary rise, although movement through real soil also depends on pore connectivity and other forces.

This helps explain how water occupies and moves through small spaces in soil and cellulose-rich plant cell walls. Gravity opposes upward rise. A capillary eventually reaches an equilibrium; it does not lift an unlimited column. In a tall tree, use the transpiration–cohesion explanation from the previous section.

Cellulose has many polar hydroxyl groups, which can form hydrogen bonds with water. Water therefore wets these surfaces. At a meniscus, surface tension acting along a wettable wall has an upward component; the rise stops when the forces balance the column’s weight. Narrower ideal tubes rise higher, but that does not imply faster flow through every real soil.
sections.revisionSummary: Adhesion to polar/charged surfaces + cohesion and surface tension → capillary movement in soil pores and plant cell walls.
terms: Capillary action: movement in narrow wettable spaces

sections.exampleTitle: A cell wall works as a wick

sections.explanation:
A solvent disperses solute particles in a solution. The polar regions of water orient around charged ions: oxygen faces a positive ion, while hydrogens face a negative ion. These ion–dipole attractions help stabilize separated ions when an appropriate salt dissolves. An ion–water attraction is not automatically a hydrogen bond.

Many small polar molecules, such as glucose, can form favorable interactions, including hydrogen bonds, with water. Solubility depends on the balance of solute–solute, water–water and solute–water interactions; polarity is a useful predictor rather than a guarantee that any quantity will dissolve.

Dissolved mineral ions move in xylem; glucose and other hydrophilic solutes travel in plasma. Most enzymes catalyse reactions in aqueous conditions. Hydrophobic substances, such as many lipids, do not mix readily with water. This is biologically useful: membrane lipid tails associate away from water, helping create a barrier while their hydrophilic heads interact with it.

For a salt crystal to dissolve, ions must separate from the crystal and water molecules must rearrange around them. Hydration stabilizes the dispersed ions, but the overall balance of interactions and dispersal determines how much dissolves. At saturation, extra solid can remain. A hydrophilic material can also absorb or interact with water without dissolving completely.

Hydrophobic does not mean that water actively pushes oil away with a special repulsive force. Nonpolar regions lack the favourable interactions that ions and many polar groups make with water; association reduces their exposure to it. The useful biological consequence is compartmentalization, rather than every useful cellular substance being water-soluble.

Oxygen is nonpolar and only slightly soluble in water. A small amount can dissolve in blood plasma, but haemoglobin in red blood cells greatly increases the amount of oxygen blood can carry by binding oxygen reversibly. This is different from glucose or mineral ions travelling dissolved in the aqueous phase. Carbon dioxide is more soluble and can also react with water; in blood, much is carried as hydrogencarbonate. The solvent therefore sets useful possibilities and limits—water does not transport every substance equally well.
sections.revisionSummary: Water hydrates ions and interacts with many polar solutes. Solubility supports metabolism/transport; hydrophobic regions help form membranes.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does salt dissolve while oil separates?

teachingBlocks.title: Water can stabilize separated ions
teachingBlocks.explanation: A solvent disperses solute particles in a solution. The polar regions of water orient around charged ions: oxygen faces a positive ion, while hydrogens face a negative ion. These ion–dipole attractions help stabilize separated ions when an appropriate salt dissolves. An ion–water attraction is not automatically a hydrogen bond.

teachingBlocks.title: Polar solutes and the limits of dissolution
teachingBlocks.explanation: Many small polar molecules, such as glucose, can form favorable interactions, including hydrogen bonds, with water. Solubility depends on the balance of solute–solute, water–water and solute–water interactions; polarity is a useful predictor rather than a guarantee that any quantity will dissolve.

teachingBlocks.title: Metabolism, transport and membrane boundaries
teachingBlocks.explanation: Dissolved mineral ions move in xylem; glucose and other hydrophilic solutes travel in plasma. Most enzymes catalyse reactions in aqueous conditions. Hydrophobic substances, such as many lipids, do not mix readily with water. This is biologically useful: membrane lipid tails associate away from water, helping create a barrier while their hydrophilic heads interact with it.

teachingBlocks.title: Why adding more solute may not dissolve it
teachingBlocks.explanation: For a salt crystal to dissolve, ions must separate from the crystal and water molecules must rearrange around them. Hydration stabilizes the dispersed ions, but the overall balance of interactions and dispersal determines how much dissolves. At saturation, extra solid can remain. A hydrophilic material can also absorb or interact with water without dissolving completely.

teachingBlocks.title: Hydrophobic association is not electrostatic repulsion
teachingBlocks.explanation: Hydrophobic does not mean that water actively pushes oil away with a special repulsive force. Nonpolar regions lack the favourable interactions that ions and many polar groups make with water; association reduces their exposure to it. The useful biological consequence is compartmentalization, rather than every useful cellular substance being water-soluble.

teachingBlocks.title: Why blood needs more than dissolved oxygen
teachingBlocks.explanation: Oxygen is nonpolar and only slightly soluble in water. A small amount can dissolve in blood plasma, but haemoglobin in red blood cells greatly increases the amount of oxygen blood can carry by binding oxygen reversibly. This is different from glucose or mineral ions travelling dissolved in the aqueous phase. Carbon dioxide is more soluble and can also react with water; in blood, much is carried as hydrogencarbonate. The solvent therefore sets useful possibilities and limits—water does not transport every substance equally well.

features.label: Na+ hydration
features.explanation: Water's partially negative oxygen faces the positive sodium ion. Ion–dipole attraction helps stabilize hydrated Na+ in solution.

features.label: Cl− hydration
features.explanation: Water's partially positive hydrogen ends orient towards negative chloride ions. A hydration shell is not a set of new O–H covalent bonds.

features.label: Cellulose fibre
features.explanation: Cellulose contains polar hydroxyl groups and interacts well with water, but its extended polymer structure and extensive intermolecular contacts prevent ordinary bulk dissolution.

features.label: Membrane lipid tails
features.explanation: Nonpolar lipid tails associate away from water as polar heads remain water-facing. Hydrophobic assembly helps maintain a cellular boundary; it is not a special electrostatic repulsion.

Oxygen dissolves only slightly, so blood uses haemoglobin to carry much more of it.

An oil droplet behaves differently because its largely nonpolar molecules lack the same favourable interactions with water.

concepts.explanation: Nonpolar regions do not make the same favourable interactions with water as ions and many polar groups. Their association reduces exposure to water; a special repulsive force is not needed. This contributes to membrane formation.

concepts.title: Transport has solubility limits
concepts.explanation: Only a small amount of oxygen dissolves in plasma. Reversible binding to haemoglobin in red blood cells greatly increases blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity. This differs from glucose or ions travelling dissolved in the aqueous fluid.

sections.explanation:
Pressure is greater at a greater depth, so the resultant fluid force on an immersed body acts upwards. Its magnitude equals the weight of displaced fluid. Water is much denser than air under comparable everyday conditions, so the same displaced volume produces much more upthrust. A swimming ringed seal gains support from water; on ice, contact with the ice supports its weight instead. Buoyancy does not require a water–air surface and is distinct from surface tension.

Dynamic viscosity measures resistance to layers of fluid sliding past one another; its SI unit is Pa s. Water has higher dynamic viscosity than air near room temperature. A moving animal also experiences drag that depends on density, speed, size and shape. A streamlined seal or black-throated loon reduces resistance, while the loon’s webbed feet push water backwards to generate forward thrust. Avoid attributing all drag to viscosity alone.

Thermal conductivity concerns heat transfer down a temperature gradient, with units W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. Under comparable everyday conditions, water conducts heat more readily than air. For the same insulating geometry and gradient this increases conductive heat loss from a warm body. Seal blubber and air trapped in a bird’s plumage reduce transfer. In a swimming animal, convection and water movement matter too; conductivity alone cannot give its total cooling rate.

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to warm unit mass by one degree, measured in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Water’s hydrogen-bond network rearranges as it warms, contributing to its high specific heat capacity. For equal mass and energy input without a phase change, ΔT = Q/(mc): a larger c gives a smaller rise. Aquatic habitats can buffer rapid temperature changes, helping seals and diving birds, although depth, mixing and energy input also affect real temperatures. High heat capacity is not thermal insulation.

explorer.prompt: Pick the property that best explains each effect, then distinguish it from the other three. Conditions matter when comparing air and water.

features.label: Immersed support
features.explanation: Buoyancy depends on the weight of displaced fluid. For an equal displaced volume, denser water usually provides greater upthrust than air; flotation still depends on the body’s average density.

features.label: Moving through fluid
features.explanation: Dynamic viscosity describes shear resistance, not every source of drag. A swimmer's speed also depends on fluid density, body shape, propulsion and flow.

features.label: Heat transfer
features.explanation: Thermal conductivity measures how readily energy passes through a material under a temperature gradient (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Conductivity alone cannot predict an animal's cooling rate.

features.label: Temperature buffering
features.explanation: Specific heat capacity measures energy per unit mass per unit temperature increase (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). A high value reduces temperature change for equal heat input; it does not itself insulate a seal.

support.simple: Water gives stronger buoyant support than air for the same displaced volume. It has higher dynamic viscosity, so moving through it brings different resistance. It also conducts heat more readily, creating a cooling challenge, but its higher specific heat capacity means more energy is needed to warm a given mass by one degree. Ringed-seal blubber and air trapped in a loon’s plumage help limit heat loss; streamlined bodies and propulsive limbs help movement. Each property explains a different demand.
support.example: A ringed seal in water receives upward support from the fluid it displaces, but it also loses heat to that water. Blubber helps reduce heat transfer. A black-throated loon uses webbed feet to push water backward, streamlining to reduce resistance, and trapped air in its plumage for insulation.
support.different: Ask four separate questions. What supports the animal’s weight? Consider buoyancy. What resists motion through the fluid? Consider viscosity together with the other causes of drag. A single word such as “thick” cannot answer all four.

concepts.title: Heat capacity is not insulation
concepts.explanation: Specific heat capacity describes energy per mass per temperature change. Thermal conductivity describes heat transfer down a temperature gradient. Water has high values of both: it can buffer temperature change while still conducting heat away from a warm animal.

concepts.title: Buoyancy versus surface tension
concepts.explanation: Buoyancy is the resultant upward force from fluid pressure and equals the weight of displaced fluid. It acts on an animal fully underwater. Surface tension concerns the water–air interface and is a different source of support for very small surface-dwelling organisms.

concepts.title: Viscosity is not every kind of drag
concepts.explanation: Viscosity is resistance to fluid layers sliding past one another. Drag also depends on density, speed and shape. Streamlining and useful propulsive surfaces help seals and loons move through water, but their total resistance cannot be calculated from viscosity alone.

sections.explanation:
The required origin hypothesis in this syllabus is delivery by asteroids. Early Earth accreted material from the Solar System, and impacts by water-bearing asteroidal material could contribute water or water-forming ingredients. Water need not have arrived as liquid droplets; hydrated minerals can carry it chemically bound.

Hydrogen occurs as isotopes. Protium has one proton and no neutron in its nucleus; deuterium has one proton and one neutron. Comparing deuterium-to-protium ratios in water-bearing meteoritic material with those in Earth’s water can help test delivery hypotheses. A similar ratio is compatible with a contribution from that material, but a match alone does not identify the proportion delivered or prove that there was only one source. The course focuses on the asteroid hypothesis; this is an example of how evidence can support it.

Water-bearing material in samples from asteroid Bennu provides evidence that asteroids can carry water-bearing minerals. This makes delivery plausible; it does not measure the fraction of Earth’s oceans supplied by asteroids or establish a single exclusive origin. Researchers continue to investigate Earth’s initial ingredients and later delivery. Recent work on hydrogen in Earth-like meteorites is a reminder that the scientific account remains open to revision.

Earth’s gravity helped retain its water inventory, and cooling allowed water vapor to condense into liquid. Long-term availability of water supported the evolution of life over billions of years. Retention is not absolute: water and hydrogen can be lost, and temperature matters. For this understanding, focus on gravity and temperatures suitable for condensation rather than learning advanced planetary chemistry.

sections.explanation:
All known cellular life depends on liquid water, so searching for it helps prioritize potentially habitable environments. The circumstellar habitable zone, or Goldilocks zone, is the range of distances where surface liquid water could persist on a suitable planet under appropriate atmospheric conditions.

The zone depends on the star’s energy output. Orbital position alone cannot establish surface liquid water: atmospheric pressure and composition also affect conditions. A planet in the zone might be barren. Detecting water vapor does not automatically mean an ocean exists, and detecting liquid water would not establish that organisms are present.

When a planet transits its star, some starlight may pass through the planet’s atmosphere. Molecules absorb characteristic wavelengths, so an atmospheric transmission spectrum can provide evidence for water vapour when the observations and models support that interpretation. Such a spectrum does not directly photograph surface water, an ocean or organisms. Distinguish the observation, a proposed molecule and the stronger claim of habitability. This is an application of evidence interpretation, beyond simply naming the Goldilocks zone.

Europa illustrates a useful limit to a surface-based definition. It is far from the Sun’s conventional habitable zone, but internal heating can allow a subsurface ocean beneath ice. The Galileo mosaic shows the icy surface, not organisms or a photograph of that ocean. Treat water as one habitability clue alongside energy and suitable chemistry; make claims no stronger than their evidence.
sections.revisionSummary: The Goldilocks zone identifies possible surface liquid-water conditions. Suitable atmosphere still matters. Water supports habitability; it is not proof of life.

concepts.title: What spectroscopy detects
concepts.explanation: Molecules absorb particular wavelengths. During a transit, atmospheric absorption may support an interpretation that water vapour is present. The observation does not by itself establish surface liquid water or organisms.

concepts.title: Why Europa is useful
concepts.explanation: Internal heating can allow a subsurface ocean beneath ice far outside the Sun’s conventional surface habitable zone. The surface mosaic shows ice, not that ocean or organisms. Water is a habitability clue, not evidence sufficient to establish life.

sections.exampleTitle: A water signature is a limited claim
sections.activityTitle: Keep the conclusion within the evidence

questions.prompt: A soluble substrate cannot easily reach an enzyme in a dried cell. Which role has water lost?

options.text: A mobile aqueous medium.
options.feedback: Correct: dissolution and movement in an aqueous phase help reactants meet.

options.text: It acts as a catalyst for every cellular reaction.
options.feedback: An aqueous medium helps reactants move; it does not catalyse every reaction.

options.text: It prevents all reactants from colliding.
options.feedback: Dissolved particles move and collide; a medium does not prevent encounters.

options.text: Dissolved substances no longer need to collide.
options.feedback: Reactants still need to meet; water enables movement rather than eliminating collisions.

questions.prompt: Which student drawing represents water correctly?

options.text: A straight H–O–H molecule with full ionic charges.
options.feedback: Water is bent and the labeled charges are partial.

options.text: Bent H₂O molecules with partial charges and a dashed H···O link.
options.feedback: Correct: distinguish polar covalent O–H from intermolecular H···O.

options.text: An O–O covalent link between separate H₂O molecules.
options.feedback: The two water molecules do not share an O–O covalent bond.

options.text: The hydrogens carry full +1 ionic charges.
options.feedback: These are partial charges: a neutral H₂O molecule has unequal sharing, not complete transfer.

questions.prompt: A continuous xylem column is pulled from its top. Why can the pull reach water below?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds supply the energy for a pump in each vessel.
options.feedback: Hydrogen bonds contribute cohesion, while evaporation drives the tension. They are not pumps.

options.text: Water becomes a rigid lattice throughout the vessel.
options.feedback: The column remains liquid, with hydrogen bonds continually rearranging.

options.text: Cohesive attractions couple neighboring water molecules.
options.feedback: Correct: cohesion helps transmit tension through the liquid.

options.text: Adhesion alone creates the pulling force at the leaf.
options.feedback: Evaporation generates tension; adhesion supports wall interactions but does not replace it.

questions.prompt: Water enters tiny wettable spaces in a plant cell wall. What is the direct role of adhesion?

options.text: Providing attraction only between water molecules.
options.feedback: That is cohesion; both contribute to capillary behavior.

options.text: Generating transpiration tension at the leaf surface.
options.feedback: Evaporation generates the tension. Adhesion is attraction between water and a different material.

options.text: All surfaces attract water equally strongly.
options.feedback: Wetting depends on the surface chemistry; polar or charged groups favor adhesion.

options.text: Attracting water to polar wall material.
options.feedback: Correct: adhesion is attraction between different substances.

questions.prompt: Which feature most helps glucose interact with water?

options.text: Its polar hydroxyl groups.
options.feedback: Correct: polar groups can interact favorably, including hydrogen bonding.

options.text: Its carbon atoms giving the entire molecule a full ionic charge.
options.feedback: Glucose is not an ion overall; its polar hydroxyl groups permit favourable water interactions.

options.text: A large entirely nonpolar surface with no polar groups.
options.feedback: An entirely nonpolar surface would not explain hydrophilicity.

options.text: All substances containing hydroxyl groups dissolve in unlimited amounts.
options.feedback: Hydrogen bonding helps, but overall structure, conditions and saturation still matter.

questions.prompt: At constant pressure under mild conditions, equal masses of water and air absorb equal energy without phase change. Why does the water warm less?

options.text: It is more buoyant.
options.feedback: Buoyancy concerns force rather than energy per degree.

options.text: Its specific heat capacity is higher.
options.feedback: Correct: ΔT = Q/(mc); larger c gives smaller ΔT.

options.text: Its conductivity must be zero.
options.feedback: Conductivity and heat capacity are different properties.

options.text: Water must be at a higher starting temperature.
options.feedback: The comparison follows from heat capacity at equal mass and energy; it does not require a hotter start.

questions.prompt: A model of early Earth includes asteroid impacts and later cooling. Which explanation is justified?

options.text: Cooling alone proves that asteroids supplied all oceans.
options.feedback: Condensation does not identify the unique source of the water.

options.text: Gravity creates water molecules from nothing.
options.feedback: Gravity contributes to retention; it does not create matter.

options.text: Water-bearing impacts could add water; cooling allowed condensation.
options.feedback: Correct: distinguish a delivery mechanism from conditions allowing liquid water to remain.

options.text: A water-bearing mineral is evidence of living cells.
options.feedback: Water-related mineral chemistry is not evidence of organisms.

questions.prompt: Water vapor is detected on a planet in a habitable zone. What is the most careful claim?

options.text: Organisms have certainly been observed.
options.feedback: Water vapor is not a detection of organisms.

options.text: No further atmospheric measurements are useful.
options.feedback: Atmospheric pressure and composition remain important.

options.text: All planets in the zone have the same gravity.
options.feedback: The zone concerns stellar energy and possible surface water, not a fixed planetary mass or gravity.

options.text: Water is present, but a liquid ocean and life remain unconfirmed.
options.feedback: Correct: phase, surface conditions and life require additional evidence.

options.text: Polar O–H bonds → hydrogen bonds → cohesion.
options.feedback: Correct: molecular polarity enables the interactions responsible for cohesion.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds → equal electron sharing → nonpolar water.
options.feedback: Sharing is unequal; water is polar.

options.text: Adhesion → covalent bonds between water molecules.
options.feedback: Adhesion neither creates water–water covalent bonds nor means water–water attraction.

options.text: Water is polar because it has gained an extra electron.
options.feedback: Polarity is uneven electron distribution, not a net ionic charge.

questions.prompt: An animal is supported within water. Which property directly explains the upward force?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds forming a solid skin around the animal.
options.feedback: Surface tension concerns an interface; submerged buoyancy is a pressure effect.

options.text: Weight of the displaced water.
options.feedback: Correct: buoyant upthrust equals the weight of displaced fluid.

options.text: Water’s specific heat capacity.
options.feedback: Heat capacity concerns temperature change, not mechanical support.

options.text: Adhesion to a cell wall supplies the upward force on every animal.
options.feedback: Buoyancy is due to pressure forces associated with displaced fluid, not wall adhesion.

questions.prompt: Interpret the capillary model. Calculate the narrow-to-wide rise ratio, describe the trend, and explain why this does not show how a tall tree lifts water.

data.caption: Illustrative equilibrium values for clean wettable tubes at fixed temperature; teaching model, not experimental measurements.

markingPoints: Rise is greater at smaller radius; doubling radius halves rise in this model (1).
Adhesion/wetting and cohesion with surface tension explain capillary rise (1).
Tall-tree transport also requires transpiration-generated tension transmitted by cohesion; finite capillarity is insufficient (1).
questions.answer: The 0.5 mm tube rises four times as high as the 2.0 mm tube. Rise is inversely related to radius in this simplified equilibrium model. Capillarity is finite and cannot replace the transpiration–cohesion explanation.

questions.prompt: Each equal-mass sample absorbs 100 J. Calculate both temperature rises using ΔT = Q/(mc). Explain what the comparison shows and why it cannot compare thermal conductivity.

data.caption: Illustrative simplified constants for teaching; not measured results. No phase change or heat loss. Air at constant pressure.

markingPoints: Water: 100/(10 × 4.2) = 2.38 K, approximately 2.4 K (1).
Higher specific heat capacity produces a smaller rise for equal mass and energy (1).
Conductivity requires evidence about heat transfer across a gradient; this calculation measures temperature response (1).
questions.answer: Water warms by about 2.4 K and air by 10 K. A temperature difference of 1 K equals 1 °C. This illustrates heat capacity, not the rate of conduction.

questions.prompt: Explain how water’s molecular properties support water and mineral transport in a plant. Include cohesion, adhesion and a distinction between the two kinds of bond.
markingPoints: Oxygen attracts shared electrons more strongly, producing partial charges (1).
Polar covalent O–H bonds are within a molecule; hydrogen bonds connect neighboring molecules in this context (1).
Hydrogen bonding contributes to cohesion that maintains a water column (1).
Evaporation from leaves generates tension transmitted through that column (1).
Adhesion involves polar/charged wall surfaces and contributes to capillary behavior (1).
Hydration of appropriate mineral ions allows them to travel dissolved in water (1).
questions.answer: Connect each molecular feature to its consequence. Do not claim capillary action alone drives flow in a tall tree or call ion–water interactions covalent bonds.

questions.prompt: A ringed seal alternates between cold seawater and ice. Explain four consequences of water’s physical properties and connect them to life in this habitat.
markingPoints: Water provides greater buoyant support than air for a given displaced volume, helping support the swimming animal (1).
Resistance in water favors streamlining and propulsive surfaces; viscosity is one contributor and drag also depends on density and speed (1).
Greater thermal conductivity than air increases the cooling challenge; insulation reduces heat transfer (1).
Higher specific heat capacity gives a smaller temperature change for equal mass and energy, buffering habitat temperature changes (1).
questions.answer: Separate mechanical support, resistance to motion, heat transfer and energy needed for temperature change. Use the ringed seal as the named organism.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim: “A planet receiving water-bearing asteroids within its Goldilocks zone will certainly develop life.”
markingPoints: Asteroid delivery is a plausible source of water-bearing material but is not proof of a complete ocean inventory (1).
Gravity and temperatures allowing condensation help retain liquid water (1).
Zone position indicates possible surface liquid water under suitable atmospheric conditions, not guaranteed conditions (1).
Water is required by known cellular life but is not sufficient evidence that life originated or is present (1).
questions.answer: The claim is too strong. It combines a possible delivery mechanism and a conditional habitability criterion, neither of which establishes life.
